title.en: The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi

region.en: Tiring-tirang, La Campana hill, Ilocos region, Luzon, Philippines (tale's home barrio)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋伊洛克斯地區蒂陵蒂蘭與『鐘』山（故事原鄉）

texts.period: Ilocano oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48a 'The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi', eBook #8299

summary.en: The waxen Juan image traps the thieving monkey, who buys his life with a promise of service. The monkey steals money, returns the king's borrowed ganta with coins in the cracks, and builds the tale of Don Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi, richest man in the world; he frightens the Burincantadas into the well, frees their prisoners, claims their herds, and leads the crooked farmer, striped-clothed, to marry Doña Elena — the king dying of joy at his new palace, the queen broken-hearted at her ugly husband, and Juan sole ruler of two kingdoms with the monkey as chief minister.
summary.zh: 蠟像胡安黏住偷玉米的猴子；猴子以『終身效力』換得性命。牠偷錢、以藏幣的量斗抬主成名，嚇得布林坎塔達三妖跳井，釋放囚徒、接收獸群，最後把衣衫襤褸的農夫打扮成『條紋胡安』迎娶埃蓮娜公主——國王見新宮樂極而亡，王后嫌夫醜陋抑鬱而終；胡安兼併兩國，猴子拜相。

sensitivity.note: Ilocano Puss-in-Boots variant recorded by Fansler from a Gonzaga narrator (Jaro, Iloilo; tale popular among 'the inhabitants of yesterday'); archival record. Fansler derives the cycle ultimately from Buddhistic lore (the helpful monkey as Bodhisatta; Tar-Baby via the Pancavudha-jataka).

passages.text: Tiring-tirang was a barrio in the town of Tang-tang, situated at the foot of a hill called 'La Campana' because of its shape; around the hill, about a mile from the barrio, flowed the Malogo River, in which the people of the town used to bathe. It so happened that one time an epidemic broke out in the community, killing off all the inhabitants except one couple, who had an only son named Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi. When Juan had reached his twelfth year his father died, and the boy had to go to work to earn money for the support of himself and his mother; at first he followed the occupation of his father, that of fisherman, but seeing that he made little money from this, he decided to become a farmer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day Juan went to Pit-pit to buy medicine for his mother, and on his way back, seeing a flock of crows still eating his corn, he became angry: he picked up a stone about the size of his fist, crept into a bush near by, and hurled his stone with such accuracy and force that one of the crows fell dead to the ground; he tied the dead crow to a bamboo pole and planted it in the middle of his cornfield, and no sooner was he out of sight than the crows flew back to the field again — but when they saw their dead companion they flew off, and never troubled Juan again. For six months Juan had no trouble from birds; he did not know, however, that not far from his field there was a monkey (chongo) living in a large tree, which used to come to his field every day and steal two or three ears of corn. He made an image of a crooked old man like himself, covered it with sticky wax, and placed it in the middle of the field — and when the hungry monkey found it and asked courteous permission for three or four ears of corn, receiving no answer from the waxen statue, he slapped it with his right paw and stuck fast, then his left paw, then first one foot and then the other, until at last he could no longer move. Juan, who had been hiding in a bush near by, presented himself: 'Now I have caught you, you thief!' — but the monkey begged for mercy and promised that he would at some future time repay him for his kindness if he would only spare his life, so Juan set the monkey free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Master Juan, do you want to marry the king's daughter? If you do, I'll arrange everything for you,' said the monkey in April, and Juan, little thinking that what the monkey promised could be true, replied yes. The monkey stole a boy's money in the market, then went to the king's palace: 'Sir, my master, Juan, wants to borrow your ganta, for he desires to measure his money.' In three days the monkey returned the measure with three centavos stuck in the bottom — 'My master cares not for three cents. He has too much money. He is very, very rich' — and the king, much surprised to hear there was a man richer than himself, stuck four pieces of gold on the four corners of the ganta when the monkey next borrowed it, to find out who was the richer, Juan or he. Two weeks later the monkey returned the measure with a gold dollar on each corner: 'My master, Juan, returns you your ganta with a thousand thanks. He is the richest man in the world... He goes to church every morning wearing his striped (tambi-tambi) clothes. This is why he is known among his people as Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi. If you will just look out of your window to-morrow morning, you will see him pass by your garden.' The king's anger was appeased; and when the monkey added, 'My master, Juan, sends me to tell you frankly that he loves your daughter, and that, if it pleases you, he will marry her,' the king, being very desirous to get more money, at last consented without even asking his daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Frightening an old man out of his bundle of clothes by shaking a tree, the monkey dressed his master for the wedding; then he ran to the home of the Burincantadas on the summit of the hill, where he began to scoop up the ground as fast as he could: 'Our king has been defeated in the war... The princess is dead, and it is said that everybody will be killed before tomorrow noon. I am resolved to hide myself under the ground to save my life.' 'For mercy's sake, have pity on us! Tell us where we can hide!' cried the three Burincantadas, already trembling with fear — 'If you will not let me scoop out a hole here, I'll jump into the well' — and as soon as they heard the word 'well,' they all ran as fast as they could, following the monkey, shouting 'Let us jump first!' — and so they did. The monkey made a motion as if he were going to follow, but instead lifted up the biggest stone he could find and threw it down the well: 'They are dead. Ah, I have caught you!' The Burincantadas now being dead, the monkey entered their palace, found many prisoners waiting to be eaten, set them all free, and told them to clean up the palace at once: 'My brothers and sisters, if any one comes and asks you who your master is, tell him that he is Don Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi.' Then he claimed for his master the thousands of horses, cows, and sheep on the farm, and hastened to Juan: 'Throw away your plough. Let's go to the king's palace, for to-night you will be married to the princess Doña Elena.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Night came, and the palace was splendidly adorned; the princess was sitting by her father when Don Juan, dressed in his striped clothes and accompanied by the monkey, entered the gate. Soon the priest came, and the princess was called to the reception-hall — but when she saw her bridegroom she ran away in despair, crying to her father, 'Father, how dare you accept as my husband such a base, dirty, crooked man! Look at him! Why, he is the meanest of the mean.' But the king replied, 'He is rich. If you don't marry him, I'll punish you very severely,' and the princess had to obey her father; but before giving her hand to Juan Pusong she said, 'O God! Let me die.' When the marriage ceremony was over, they set out by carriage for Don Juan's palace; four hours passed, and still no palace was to be seen — 'Monkey, if what you have said to me is not true, your head shall answer for your lie' — but then the shepherds answered that the herds were all owned by Don Juan Pusong, and the palace came in sight, so magnificent that the king said, 'Why, it is not a palace; it is heaven itself.' Upstairs the king confessed, 'I am not the richest man on earth' — and soon he died of joy, his body being placed in a golden coffin and buried in the church. The couple inherited his dominion; but Queen Elena could not endure her ugly husband, and two weeks later she died broken-hearted — so Juan was left as sole ruler of two kingdoms, and the monkey became his chief minister.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'The Monkey and Juan Pusong Tambi-tambi'; not verbatim.

region.en: San Carlos, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines (story popular among the Pangasinanes)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦阿西楠省聖卡洛斯（邦阿西楠人流行故事）

texts.period: Pangasinan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48b 'Andres the Trapper', eBook #8299

summary.en: Andres, an orphan trapper, spares a monkey caught in his snare; the grateful animal sells his wild chickens, borrows the rich Don Toribio's measures with coins stuck in the cracks to prove his master counts his money, dresses Andres in shoes and ready-made clothes, teaches him elegance, and marries him to the most beautiful girl in the province — Aning — whose inheritance he commands when Don Toribio dies.
summary.zh: 孤兒捕鳥人安德烈斯放了陷在網中的猴子；知恩的猴子替他賣野雞、向富紳東·托里比奧借斗量錢——斗縫裡嵌滿銀幣，謠言遂起。猴子為他添置鞋帽新衣、教他舉止談吐，終促成他與全省最美的姑娘阿寧的婚事；東·托里比奧死後，安德烈斯繼承全部家產。

sensitivity.note: Pangasinan Puss-in-Boots variant recorded by Fansler from a Perez narrator (San Carlos); archival record. Fansler notes the monkey takes the place of the cat, fox, or jackal of other traditions, and connects the animal's gratitude to Buddhistic lore.

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived in a village a poor widow who had an only son named Andres; they lived in a small hut situated near the Patacbo forest. When Andres was between twelve and thirteen years old his mother died, and from then on he lived alone in his mean little hut, where he had to cook his own food and wash his own clothes. One morning some boys invited Andres to go to the woods with them to trap; his companions set their traps in the places where the wild chickens used to feed, and when they returned in the afternoon each trap had caught a wild cock. Andres became envious of his companions, took his knife and made two traps of his own, and found two wild cocks snared the next morning; he sold one and ate the other for his dinner, made many more traps, and from then on made his living by trapping, often catching as many as fifteen birds in a day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'Andres the Trapper'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, after Andres had been a trapper for many years, he went to the forest as usual to see what he had caught, and found that his traps had been moved and that in one of them was a big monkey caught by the leg. As Andres was about to kill the monkey with a big stick, the animal said to him, 'My dear Andres, don't harm me! And I will be your helper by and by.' Andres was much astonished to hear the monkey talk; he was moved to pity and set the animal free, and when he started toward his home the monkey followed him — from then on they lived together, and soon the monkey learned how to sell wild chickens in the market.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'Andres the Trapper'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In that town there lived a very rich man by the name of Toribio, who had a daughter named Aning; the people considered Aning the most beautiful lady in the province, but none of the young men of the town courted Aning, for they felt unworthy and ashamed to woo the richest and most beautiful girl. One fine day the monkey went to town and sold wild chickens as usual; on his way home he stopped at Don Toribio's house and said that his master had sent him to borrow their money-measure — 'Don't you know? Don Andres, a very rich, handsome young gentleman who lives in the valley of Obong.' Don Toribio at once lent the ganta-measure to the monkey, who, before returning it to the owner the next morning, put a peso, a fifty-centavo piece, a peseta, and a media-peseta in the cracks of the measure. 'Has your master finished measuring his money?' — 'No, sir! We have not finished; but this box is too small, and it takes us too long to measure with it' — and Don Toribio brought a cavan, which equals about twenty-five gantas, for the monkey to keep till the next day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'Andres the Trapper'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Ah, me! What money are you going to count? Don't you know that we are very poor?' said Andres when he saw the large measure. 'Let me manage things, Andres, and I promise you that you shall marry the beautiful daughter of the rich man,' said the monkey. The following day Andres caught many wild chickens, and when the monkey had sold them all in the market he went back to their hut and took the cavan he had borrowed, sticking money in the cracks before returning it to Don Toribio, as he had done to the first measure. 'I am the richest man in town, yet I cannot throw money away like the master of this fellow,' said Don Toribio to himself; 'perhaps he is even richer than I am.' When the monkey was about to take his leave, the rich man told him to tell his master to come there on the third day; the monkey stopped at the market on his way home to buy a pair of shoes, some ready-made clothes, and a hat for Andres, and in three days had taught Andres how to walk easily with shoes on, how to speak elegantly, how to eat with a spoon and fork and knife, and how to tell Don Toribio that he wanted to marry his daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'Andres the Trapper'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the time came, Andres and the monkey set out for the town; they were welcomed by Don Toribio and his daughter Aning, and after a short talk Andres spoke of his purpose in coming there — he wanted to marry Don Toribio's daughter. Don Toribio gladly accepted the offer and said that the wedding would be held the next morning; hasty preparations were made for the ceremony, and in the morning a priest came, and Andres and Aning were married. Many guests were present, and everybody had a good time. A few years later Don Toribio died, and Andres inherited all his wealth; he then became a very rich man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 48 'Andres the Trapper'; not verbatim.

title.en: Juan the Fool: The Dead Wife, the Crabs, and the Lizard
title.zh: 糊塗胡安：死妻、螃蟹與蜥蜴

region.en: Bocawe, Bulakan, Luzon, Philippines (where the story was told at a barrio gathering)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋布拉克省博卡維（ barrio 聚會所講的故事）

texts.period: Tagalog noodle-tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool', eBook #8299

summary.en: Told to take a quiet, tongue-tied wife, Juan finds a corpse in bed; told that 'those who stink are dead,' he buries his napping mother and floats downstream on a banana raft as a dead man himself. Housekeeper to robbers, he kills a murmuring pot that mocks him, sends two dozen crabs swimming across the river 'straight home,' falls on a lizard and cries 'Tao, tao!' in terror — until, living in a mango-tree, he drops his bamboo table on two money-bearers and makes off with the bag, buying a house, a carabao, and a cart.
summary.zh: 奉母命娶『安靜寡言』之妻的胡安，抱回一具女屍；學得『發臭者必死』的教訓後，他埋葬了午睡的母親，又自認已死，乘香蕉筏順流漂去。為強盜當家：他打死『嘲笑他』的沸鍋、讓廿四隻螃蟹『自行游回家』、被蜥蜴落背嚇得喊『有人！有人！』——直到棲身芒果樹上，他把竹桌砸向兩個帶錢人，席捲錢袋，置屋置牛置車而去。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog noodle-tale recorded by Fansler from a Mendoza narrator (story from Bulakan, told at an informal barrio gathering); archival record.

passages.text: Juan is twenty years old, and at this age begins to become famous in his little barrio: short in stature, with very black eyes that slowly roll in their sockets, a narrow mouth, a double chin, a short flat nose, a broad forehead, thick lips, black straight hair, a body round like a pumpkin, and short legs — he seems to be always tired, yet he is invited to every bayluhan and katapusan because he is sure to bring with him laughter and merriment. Juan lives in a poor barrio which consists of a few poor nipa huts, with a small chapel of stone with a turret and bells, a cross erected in the courtyard, and a rivulet just outside the village hidden in a thick forest extending to the foot of a mountain. At the time the story opens Juan is eating his breakfast with his mother, an old widow whose sole ambition is to establish Juan in a good social position; she is constantly advising her son that a good wife is always quiet and tongue-tied, and does not go noisily about the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As Juan is an obedient son, he soon determines to get him a good wife; after a short time he comes home to his mother and says, 'Mother, I have found the girl you will like — the one who shall be my wife. She is speechless and motionless. Her eyes are staring in just one place. Though I have watched her closely for about twelve hours, I have not observed the slightest motion in her lips and eyelids. She remained quiet in her bed, although there were many noisy people in the house.' 'And is that all?' says his mother. 'No, mother... Her hands were very cold. She was deaf, and she did not answer me. This fact makes her all the lovelier... There is only one thing you did not tell me, however. The girl had a stinking waxy-like odor.' 'O Juan! I already suspected from your long description that you followed my instructions too literally. The girl you found is a dead one. Now, remember: those who stink are dead.' 'Thanks, mother. I will never forget that.' A few days later, when Juan and his mother are eating their breakfast, Juan smells a stinking odor; as he does not see anyone else in the little room, he thinks that his mother is dead. Then, when his mother is taking her siesta, Juan says to himself, 'Surely mother is dead'; he goes out quietly and digs a grave for her, buries her in it, and mourns for her nine days — now Juan is alone in the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One morning, when Juan is eating his breakfast by himself, he smells again a stinking odor; he looks around, and, as he does not see anyone, he thinks that he himself is dead. There is nobody to bury him, so he goes to the river, takes five or six banana-trunks, and makes a raft of them; he lies down on the raft and lets the current of the river carry him away. In three hours the current has carried him into the woods, where all of a sudden he is called in a fierce voice by the captain of a band of robbers; Juan does not stir in his place, but sadly tells the robbers that he is a dead man — until the captain frightens him, saying he will shoot if he does not get up. As Juan does not care for the taste of bullets, he goes to the bank of the river, still thinking that he is a walking dead body, and goes with the robbers into the woods, where the captain appoints Juan their housekeeper, ordering him to cook rice but to keep very still and quiet, for they may be caught by the Spanish soldiers (cazadores).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Juan shuts the windows, and everything is quiet and undisturbed; he even tries to control his breathing for fear of the noise it may make. Cautiously he takes an earthen pot and puts rice and water into it, places the pot on the fire, and sits down near it — everything is silent until suddenly a murmuring sound seems to come from the pot (the water is beginning to boil). Juan thinks that the pot is saying, 'Buluk ka' — 'You are decayed' — and gets very angry; he whispers to the pot to stop, but the sound becomes louder and louder, until at last, exasperated, he takes a piece of bamboo-bellows and gives the pot a fatal blow, putting an end to the pot, the rice, and the flames. At noon the hungry robbers come home to find Juan almost breathless in the darkest corner of the house, the pot broken and the rice scattered over the floor; Juan says that the naughty pot was making too much noise and mocking him, and the captain cannot help smiling at Juan's foolishness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day the captain gives Juan some money and tells him to go to the market to buy some earthen pots and some crabs; Juan buys all the crabs he can find and about two dozen large earthen pots, then threads them all on a long piece of sharpened rattan to carry them easily. Soon he comes to a large, wide river with a very strong current: he remembers that crabs are good swimmers, so he decides to untie them and let them swim to the other side. 'Now, crabs, we have to cross this broad river. I know that you are good swimmers... Please swim to the other side of the river as quickly as you can, for I cannot carry you. If you reach the other side before I do, you may go straight home, or wait for me' — and he is very glad to see them swim so fast. He looks around for the crabs, but, seeing none, he says to himself, 'Perhaps they have become tired of waiting for me and have gone straight home, as I ordered them to do. What a surprise for the captain!' — and when he finds out that not one of the naughty crabs obeyed him, he blames himself for his quiet nature and swears that he will never trust a crab again; when the robbers see the holes in the bottom of all the pots they cannot help laughing, and the captain addresses Juan with all the epithets found in a common slang dictionary. Several days later the captain calls Juan one night to rob a certain house, and says, 'Juan, go into the silong of the house, and see if the people are awake. Now, remember, if you feel something hot, it is a man; but if it is cold, it is a bolo.' After a while something hot falls on Juan's back; he quickly runs away crying, 'Tao, tao!' — 'Man, man!' — and all the robbers flee too. When the robbers light a match they see only a little lizard clinging to Juan's worn-out camisa; the captain tells Juan he may go away, for he is not worth anything.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Juan leaves the band of robbers and decides to live up in a tree, because he is all alone: he takes a low bamboo table and goes up into a very large mango-tree, choosing a well-hidden place, and ties his table firmly to the branches; he spends the day in the neighboring towns looking for food, but at night he comes back to the tree and sleeps there. Early one morning Juan wakes up and hears faint whispers: he looks down and sees two men talking very earnestly together, one of them carrying a bag of money. Juan loosens his table and lets it fall on the men; it makes a loud crash, and they run away. Juan quickly climbs down the tree and makes off with the bag of money. He now decides to live in town: after he has found a barrio that suits him, he buys a house, a carabao, and a cart, and lives peacefully in his new house — sometimes he works, but he spends most of his time sleeping, for he is a very lazy fellow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 49 'Juan the Fool'; not verbatim.
